vignette:
Rajesh was thirty-two when the men came to the compound in the Philippines. He had been working as a conservation volunteer in a remote region, part of a three-month assignment cataloguing endemic bird species in a protected forest area. The work had been demanding but purposeful-he was good at it, methodical, patient with the painstaking detail required to document migration patterns. On the third week, armed militants swept through the compound at dawn. They took four foreigners, including Rajesh. For nineteen days he was held in a makeshift camp, moved twice, kept in a concrete room with a single barred window. The room was small enough that he could touch both walls if he stretched his arms. They wanted money. They wanted statements. What they wanted shifted daily depending on who was guarding him and what news filtered in from outside. The uncertainty was its own kind of captivity-not knowing whether today would bring negotiation or punishment, whether the sounds of shouting outside meant rescue or execution. During those nineteen days, he was beaten twice, once across the shoulders and ribs when he refused to repeat a statement for a video, and once across the hands when he tried to block his face during an interrogation. When he was finally released through a ransom payment and diplomatic intervention, he weighed fourteen pounds less than when he went in, and his left shoulder carried a dull ache that never fully resolved.

That was nine years ago. For the first six months after his release, Rajesh told himself he was fine, that he was lucky, that others had endured worse. He returned to the States, took a job with the National Park Service, and moved to a quiet region in the Pacific Northwest. He met Priya through a hiking group three years ago, and they had built a careful, quiet life together. But the careful life was increasingly a life of avoidance, and by the time Rajesh turned forty-one, the avoidance had become architecture. At work, Rajesh had gradually shifted his patrol routes to avoid the ranger station where his supervisor, Captain Morrison, held his office hours. Morrison wore the campaign hat and uniform that came with the position, and something about the sight of him-the authority implicit in the fabric and insignia-sent Rajesh into a state of hypervigilance that made his shifts unbearable. He had taken to doing his paperwork at home, arriving before Morrison came in, leaving after he departed. His supervisor had begun to notice, had asked if everything was all right. Rajesh had said yes, of course, while internally calculating how to keep his job without having to see Morrison's face. When a documentary about military operations had aired on the news, Rajesh had felt his chest tighten at the opening credits. He had quietly asked Priya if they could watch something else, and when she had gently suggested that avoidance might not help, he had agreed with her immediately, apologized, and then felt a flash of resentment at her for making him feel foolish. He found himself unable to listen to news broadcasts if they mentioned armed conflict or hostage situations; he would change the station or leave the room entirely, his heart already accelerating before the full story could register. Loud noises-a car backfiring, a motorcycle engine-would send him rigid with the certainty that danger was imminent, though he could never quite articulate why a sound from the street held the weight of a threat.

The flashbacks came without warning, and they carried with them a physicality that confused him. A car backfiring near the trailhead sent him into a crouch, his body convinced for several seconds that the sound was gunfire. But it was the unexpected movements that sometimes undid him most completely. Last month, Priya had turned quickly from the kitchen counter to hand him a plate, and his entire body had seized-his hands flew up defensively, his breath caught, and for a moment he could not process that it was her, that he was safe, that a sudden motion was not a threat. She had frozen, the plate still extended, and they had both stood there while his nervous system caught up to reality. He would be walking through the forest-the work he loved-and suddenly he was back in the concrete room, the light through the barred window the same slant as the light coming through the trees, and his body would seize with the certainty that he was still there, that the nine years had not happened. These moments left him shaken, disoriented, and increasingly certain that his own mind could not be trusted. Even when Priya held his hand and told him he was safe, that they were in their home, he could not believe her. His body knew something she didn't. The memories themselves had taken on a quality that made him question what was real-sometimes they felt as vivid and immediate as the present moment, as though the concrete room existed in the same temporal space as his living room, and he could slip between them without warning. What troubled him most was that during these flashbacks, the old pain would return. His left shoulder-the one beaten across the ribs-would begin to ache with a sharp, specific tenderness, as though the blow had just landed. His hands would throb with the memory of being struck, a phantom pain that arrived alongside the visual recall, his body insisting that the beating was happening again, that this time was indistinguishable from that time. He had come to believe that his mind was fundamentally damaged, that the trauma had rewired something essential in him that could never be restored to factory condition.

For the past two years, Rajesh had restricted his eating to a rigid schedule and strict portions. It was the one thing he could control absolutely-what went in, when, how much. Everything else felt permeable, vulnerable to invasion. He had lost weight again, not dramatically, but enough that Priya had asked him to see a doctor. He had, and the doctor found nothing wrong. What the doctor could not measure was the small, hard satisfaction Rajesh felt when he closed the refrigerator without eating the extra portion, when his hunger became proof that he still had dominion over something. He had also begun to fantasize about the men who held him. Not constantly, but in the quiet moments before sleep, he would construct scenarios in which he found them, in which they experienced a fraction of what he had experienced, in which his powerlessness was reversed into absolute control. These fantasies were vivid and satisfying in a way that troubled him-he was not a violent man, or so he had always believed. He found himself preoccupied with thoughts of revenge, with imagined confrontations that never resolved but only cycled through variations, each one leaving him more tense than the last. He was hyperaware of his surroundings on patrol, scanning constantly for threats, his attention fractured between the present landscape and the vigilance required to stay safe. Sleep had become unreliable-he would lie awake for hours or wake gasping from nightmares he could not quite remember but could feel in his chest for the rest of the day.

What finally brought Rajesh to therapy was a moment at work that felt like a reckoning. A new ranger, fresh out of training, had mentioned casually that his brother was in the Army, that he was proud of the military service in his family. Rajesh had felt something crack open in his chest. He had nodded and smiled and said the right things, but afterward he had sat in his truck for an hour, unable to move, thinking that he was forever separated from normal human conversation, that he would never be able to hear about the military without feeling like a coward, like someone who had failed a test of courage that others passed without even knowing it was being administered. He had called Priya that night and told her he needed help, that something was broken and he didn't know how to fix it. What frightened him most was not the flashbacks themselves, but the possibility that they would never stop, that at forty-one he would spend the rest of his life flinching at sudden movements, avoiding his own supervisor, unable to watch the news without his chest tightening, his shoulder aching with a pain that belonged to the past but lived in his present. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to articulate it, was that he might someday trust his body again, that he might walk through the forest without waiting for the concrete room to swallow him whole, and that the old beating might finally remain only in memory, no longer insisting on its reality through the language of his flesh.

Even when Priya held his hand and told him he was safe, that they were in their home, he could not believe her. His body knew something she didn't. The memories themselves had taken on a quality that made him question what was real—sometimes they felt as vivid and immediate as the present moment, as though the concrete room existed in the same temporal space as his living room, and he could slip between them without warning. He had come to believe that his mind was fundamentally damaged, that the trauma had rewired something essential in him that could never be restored to factory condition.

For the past two years, Rajesh had restricted his eating to a rigid schedule and strict portions. It was the one thing he could control absolutely—what went in, when, how much. Everything else felt permeable, vulnerable to invasion. He had lost weight again, not dramatically, but enough that Priya had asked him to see a doctor. He had, and the doctor found nothing wrong. What the doctor could not measure was the small, hard satisfaction Rajesh felt when he closed the refrigerator without eating the extra portion, when his hunger became proof that he still had dominion over something. He had also begun to fantasize about the men who held him. Not constantly, but in the quiet moments before sleep, he would construct scenarios in which he found them, in which they experienced a fraction of what he had experienced, in which his powerlessness was reversed into absolute control. These fantasies were vivid and satisfying in a way that troubled him—he was not a violent man, or so he had always believed. He found himself preoccupied with thoughts of revenge, with imagined confrontations that never resolved but only cycled through variations, each one leaving him more tense than the last. He was hyperaware of his surroundings on patrol, scanning constantly for threats, his attention fractured between the present landscape and the vigilance required to stay safe. Sleep had become unreliable—he would lie awake for hours or wake gasping from nightmares he could not quite remember but could feel in his chest for the rest of the day.

What finally brought Rajesh to therapy was a moment at work that felt like a reckoning. A new ranger, fresh out of training, had mentioned casually that his brother was in the Army, that he was proud of the military service in his family. Rajesh had felt something crack open in his chest. He had nodded and smiled and said the right things, but afterward he had sat in his truck for an hour, unable to move, thinking that he was forever separated from normal human conversation, that he would never be able to hear about the military without feeling like a coward, like someone who had failed a test of courage that others passed without even knowing it was being administered. He had called Priya that night and told her he needed help, that something was broken and he didn't know how to fix it. What frightened him most was not the flashbacks themselves, but the possibility that they would never stop, that at forty-one he would spend the rest of his life flinching at sudden movements, avoiding his own supervisor, unable to watch the news without his chest tightening. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to articulate it, was that he might someday trust his body again, that he might walk through the forest without waiting for the concrete room to swallow him whole.

They wanted money. They wanted statements. What they wanted shifted daily depending on who was guarding him and what news filtered in from outside. The uncertainty was its own kind of captivity—not knowing whether today would bring negotiation or punishment, whether the sounds of shouting outside meant rescue or execution. During those nineteen days, he was beaten twice, once across the shoulders and ribs when he refused to repeat a statement for a video, and once across the hands when he tried to block his face during an interrogation. Last month, Priya had turned quickly from the kitchen counter to hand him a plate, and his entire body had seized—his hands flew up defensively, his breath caught, and for a moment he could not process that it was her, that he was safe, that a sudden motion was not a threat.
